cards.title: Don't Abandon Hook Testing Because of Andromeda
cards.summary: Andromeda may group near-identical ads but rotating substantially different hooks still unlocks net-new reach for fatigued winners, so hook testing remains high-value.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep testing hooks on a fatigued winning ad or to kill it and start entirely new creative concepts.
steps: Recognize the widespread claim that Andromeda groups minor variations into single Entity IDs and therefore punishes hook testing; the source argues this leads advertisers to a mistake.
Understand that Andromeda groups visually and contextually identical ads, not every variation of a hook; the source maintains hook testing still works on live accounts.
Agree that diverse creative has always been valuable, but don't let that reasoning cancel the hook's outsized importance in paid social video.
Because the hook sells the ad, the source places roughly 90% of a creative's impact in the first 3-5 seconds, citing Ogilvy's headline logic.
Continue running hook variations on proven bodies as your default low-effort, high-ROI play rather than only producing entirely new assets.
Verify current Meta/Andromeda behavior on your own account rather than assuming the algorithm has made hook testing obsolete, because tool behavior can change.
caveats: This is the source's opinion and account experience, not a documented platform rule; confirm with your own tests.
Andromeda grouping behavior may change over time, so re-validate the assumption on live campaigns.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Revive a Fatigued Hero Ad by Replacing Only the Hook
cards.summary: A proven testimonial ad that fatigued after months can be revitalized by attaching new 3-5 second hooks rather than discarding the asset.
cards.use_when: A previously top-performing video ad (e.g. testimonial) has fatigued after extended spend and stopped scaling.
steps: Confirm the ad is genuinely fatigued: in the source's example a top performer that ran roughly six to seven months and was about 5x better than anything else began to lose results.
Instead of filming entirely new concepts, rework only the first 3-5 seconds of the proven body.
Avoid simply repurposing more hooks from the existing footage; most of your market already saw that hook and dropped off, so reuse of the same avatar/visual rarely re-engages them.
Shoot new hooks with a different person, e.g. EGC (Employee Generated Content) delivering the hook before transitioning into the original CGC (Customer Generated Content) testimonial body.
In the source's case this restored performance to prior levels at the same daily spend, and the reworked ads became the account's current top performers.
Treat these results as one account's example, not a guaranteed outcome; test your own winner before scaling spend assumptions.
caveats: The source could not show the actual client ad, so the performance figures are uncorroborated.
Results cited (5x, six-to-seven-month fatigue, restored spend) are specific to one account and not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Four Levers for Varying a Hook: Angle, Offer, Avatar, Format
cards.summary: Rotate hooks along four distinct levers—angle, offer, avatar and format—to bypass Andromeda grouping and reach genuinely new audiences.
cards.use_when: Planning hook variations for a proven ad body and choosing which dimensions to change.
steps: Lever 1 – Angle: change the messaging or contextual/seasonal framing. In the source's example the hook was made contextually relevant to the current time of year so an older-sounding testimonial felt current again.
Lever 2 – Offer: change the CTA or product focus. This often lives in the copy or headline rather than the spoken hook; e.g. pivot from a single product to a bundle or a sale.
Lever 3 – Avatar: change who delivers the hook. Using an EGC character with a very different profile from the on-screen testimonial hooks new people the original avatar missed.
Lever 4 – Format: change the first 3-4 seconds visually. Options include a 3-second static or GIF/motion-graphic intro with a written testimonial overlay that transitions into the video.
You don't need to change all four: a single lever (the source changed angle and avatar) can revitalize the ad; changing all four can also work.
Pair lever changes with volume because results depend on testing enough variations.
caveats: Combining all four levers is described as very likely to work but only 'through volume', meaning it requires producing many variations.
Changing only wording will re-hook some viewers but not everyone; a visual change is also needed for broader re-engagement.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Test More Than Three Hooks to Beat the Odds
cards.summary: Testing only two or three hook variations per concept has low odds of producing a winner; run many variations on a proven body instead.
cards.use_when: Choosing how many hook variations to produce when revitalizing a proven winning ad.
steps: Reject the trap of limiting variations out of fear that Andromeda will group them all together; that fear can push you to under-test.

If you test only an angle change and a couple of avatar changes (the source's example of three hooks), the odds of a high performer are low unless you are an exceptional scriptwriter with deep audience knowledge.
Instead produce a higher volume of hooks on the proven body; in the source's example they ran four different hooks across two bodies, reworking both hooks and body slightly.

Budget the work so the volume is achievable: making 10 versions of a 3-5 second hook is roughly the same effort as producing one ~75-second ad body, since most shooting and editing effort lives in the body.
Because the hook drives retention, concentrate repeated low-effort iterations there while keeping the proven body intact.
caveats: The claim that 'three hooks is usually too few' is the source's heuristic, not a calculated benchmark.
The 10-versions-equal-one-body effort comparison is the source's practical estimate for their own 75-second format.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Why Hooks Deserve the Budget: Drop-off Math
cards.summary: Most viewers drop off at the hook, so the first 3-5 seconds carry the highest ROI of the entire creative and justify disproportionate production effort.
cards.use_when: Allocating creative production time and budget between hooks versus full ad bodies.
steps: Apply the source's premise that roughly 80-90% of viewers drop off before the ad body, making the hook the most critical variable in retention.
Consequently, the source argues about 90% of advertising dollars are 'wasted' after the hook if the hook doesn't sell.
Invest most iteration effort in the first 3-5 seconds because improvements there affect the largest share of your audience.
Since producing multiple 3-5 second hooks is a fraction of the effort of full new ads, the source considers hook testing the highest-ROI creative activity.
Note the tension acknowledged by the source: an extremely good single hook could outperform, but the odds of hitting one are low, which is why volume in hooks is preferred.
Do not merely tweak scripts; combine script changes with angle, offer, avatar and format changes to reach new viewers.
caveats: The 80-90% drop-off figure and the 90% effort allocation are the source's stated premises, not independently verified benchmarks.
Treat the 'spend 90% of effort on the hook' framing as a directional principle, not a literal budget rule.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Distinguish EGC Hooks from CGC Bodies
cards.summary: Employee Generated Content (EGC) can deliver a new hook that leads into the original Customer Generated Content (CGC) testimonial body to re-hook audiences.
cards.use_when: Structuring a testimonial ad where the hook and testimonial come from different sources to expand reach.
steps: Define EGC as Employee Generated Content, e.g. a team member or client-side person filming the opening on-camera hook.
Define CGC as Customer Generated Content, i.e. the customer providing the core testimonial that carries the ad body.
Build the ad so a new EGC hook (a different person from the original avatar) plays first, then transitions into the proven CGC testimonial.
Use a deliberately different avatar profile in the EGC hook from the one in the body to hook viewers the original presenter never reached.
Reuse the proven body unchanged underneath, since its performance is already established; only the 3-5 second intro is new.
Pair EGC hooks with angle changes when the original body's wording or visuals feel dated.
caveats: The EGC/CGC split is the source's terminology for this hybrid structure; it is not a platform-defined format.
Source's client case is one example and results are not guaranteed.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx

cards.title: Raise the Quality Bar for Hook Variations
cards.summary: The mechanics of hook testing haven't fundamentally changed but the quality/requirement bar to make it succeed has risen, so weak or repurposed hooks should be expected to fail.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why new hooks fail on a proven ad and deciding whether to blame the method or the execution.
steps: When new hooks fail, don't conclude that hook testing no longer works or that Andromeda killed it; first check whether you reused existing footage rather than producing genuinely different hooks.
A common failure pattern: taking hooks from the existing video and repurposing them so the majority of the market has already seen and rejected them.
The goal is to re-serve the ad to the same audience with a differently delivered hook that gets them to hold and watch through.
Recognize that a wording change alone re-hooks some viewers; add visual changes to reach those who still drop off.
Assume the bar is higher now: unless you are unusually strong at scriptwriting and audience understanding, generic variations are unlikely to hit.
Decide to increase production effort and volume (e.g. a new presenter, new context, new format intro) before concluding the approach is dead.
caveats: The claim that 'the bar has gone up' is the source's qualitative observation, not a measured threshold.
Failed hooks can be caused by poor scripts or mismatched audience, not only by algorithm changes.
cards.source_name: Why Hook Testing Still Works With Andromeda.docx
